clips.title: Why non-aggregated SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY
clips.hook: Why SELECT col, COUNT(*) without GROUP BY fails, and the MySQL pitfall.
clips.summary: Any non-aggregated column in the SELECT list alongside an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY, because the DB must know how to collapse that column to one value per output row. Some older MySQL configurations (without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY) accept it and return arbitrary values from the group.
clips.videoTitle: SQL Group By: An Explanation and How To Use It

quiz.question: Why does SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders (no GROUP BY) raise an error in standard SQL?
options: The table lacks an index on product_id
product_id yields multiple values per output row, with no rule to collapse them to one
COUNT cannot be used with a column
ORDER BY is required with COUNT
quiz.explanation: The aggregate collapses all rows into one, but product_id is non-aggregated and has many values, so the result is ill-defined unless it is grouped.

clips.title: CSMA/CD: Sense, Transmit, Detect, Jam, Back Off
clips.hook: Walk through the CSMA/CD loop including jam signal and why backoff must be random.
clips.summary: A station senses the medium, transmits when idle, and keeps listening for collisions during transmission. On a collision it stops, sends a jam signal so all nodes know, then waits a random time so the colliding stations don't retry in lockstep.

quiz.question: Why must the retransmission wait time after a CSMA/CD collision be random per station?
options: To reduce the cable's signal attenuation
To let the jam signal propagate to all nodes
So the colliding stations do not retransmit simultaneously and collide again
To ensure the receiver can send an acknowledgement first
quiz.explanation: If both colliding stations waited a fixed identical time, they would retransmit together and collide repeatedly; randomization breaks the symmetry.

clips.title: CSMA/CA: Collision Avoidance in Wireless
clips.hook: Why wireless can't detect collisions, and how random backoff plus ACKs substitute for it.
clips.summary: Wireless stations cannot listen while transmitting, so they avoid collisions instead: sense the channel, defer if busy, wait a random time once idle, then send. Reliability comes from link-layer acknowledgements, and a missing ACK causes the sender to retry.

quiz.question: In CSMA/CA, how does a sender conclude that its frame was lost to a collision?
options: It detects a jam signal
It senses voltage increase on the medium
The access point sends a CTS
It does not receive an acknowledgement from the receiver
quiz.explanation: Without collision detection, the absence of an ACK is the indication of failure, triggering a retry.

clips.title: CPI Impact of a 3-Cycle Branch Penalty
clips.hook: Compute effective CPI with branch frequency, taken rate and penalty: why 3 cycles costs 45%.
clips.summary: Effective CPI = ideal CPI + branch frequency × taken fraction × taken-branch penalty. With 30% branches, 50% taken and 3-cycle penalty, CPI = 1 + 0.3×0.5×3 = 1.45, a ~45% slowdown.

quiz.question: Ideal CPI is 1, 20% of instructions are branches, 60% of branches are taken, taken penalty is 2 cycles, not-taken branches cost nothing. What is the effective CPI?

clips.title: Cutting Branch Penalty: Resolve Branches in ID
clips.hook: Move target computation and condition evaluation to ID to drop the penalty from 3 cycles to 1.
clips.summary: Reducing the penalty requires determining the outcome and the target earlier. Target needs only PC+4 and the immediate, so a dedicated adder in ID suffices. Condition evaluation must fit in a fraction of a cycle after the register read, so only simple tests (zero, equal/unequal) are supported. Complex compares like less-than are excluded to protect the critical path.

quiz.question: Why does the MIPS I ISA restrict branches to compare-with-zero and equality tests when resolving in ID?
options: The ALU is unavailable in ID
Complex comparisons would lengthen the critical path of ID and reduce clock frequency
The register file has only one read port
Less-than needs forwarding, equality does not
quiz.explanation: Branch evaluation follows the register read in the same stage, so it must be fast; magnitude compare needs a slower carry chain.

clips.title: Datapath Changes for ID-Stage Branching
clips.hook: Move the target adder to ID, add a zero-detect on RS, and handle the new forwarding and stall hazards.
clips.summary: The target adder moves to ID, taking PC+4 and the shifted sign-extended immediate. A zero-detect on the just-read RS drives the PC mux. This creates new hazards: forwarding to ID from MEM and WB producers, and a stall when the producer is in EX.

quiz.question: With branches resolved in ID, why must a stall be inserted if the branch's source register is produced by the instruction currently in EX?
options: The target adder needs the ALU
The register file is being written
The PC mux is busy
The result is not computed until the end of EX, but the branch needs it during ID in the same cycle
quiz.explanation: The EX result is not available until the cycle ends, too late for the ID-stage comparison, and forwarding can't help.
